## Notes

- No census or survey with a household-deaths module is available (the country's DHS surveys have no module on deaths of household members at all ages), so adult mortality uses the general gradient (value in the table above). Fertility and infant mortality come from the 2017 IDHS.
- Cross-check: a cohort study of the Indonesia Family Life Survey (Sudharsanan 2019, J Gerontol B 74(3), doi:10.1093/geronb/gbx061; adults aged 30–80 in 2007, followed to 2014–15, 1,443 deaths) reports odds ratios of death by quartile of a DHS-type asset index. Fitted across the quartile midpoints, they imply wealth gradients of −0.61 (urban women), −0.30 (urban men), +0.06 (rural women) and −0.45 (rural men), mean −0.32. These are for ages 30–80, where gradients are weaker than in 45q15 (see the age offsets of the general gradient), and each rests on a few hundred deaths; they are flatter than the general gradient, as expected at these ages, but too imprecise to test it. By a rough calculation from the sample size and national mortality, the survey's own microdata would hold fewer than the 900 deaths at ages 15–59 needed for a publishable estimate.
- The wealth gradient in the total fertility rate is modest, while the gradient in adolescent fertility (ages 15–19) is among the steepest in the library: the differential is concentrated in the timing of births.
